title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
directAnswer: Preorder's first element is always the root. Find that root inside inorder: everything to its left is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree, and the count of those left elements tells you how to split preorder too. Recurse. Pre-build a hash map from value → inorder index so each root lookup is O(1), and advance a single global preorder pointer. O(n) time, O(n) space.

remember.pattern: Divide & conquer on traversal arrays (root-from-preorder, split-by-inorder)
remember.formula:
idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
self.pre = 0
def build(lo, hi):           # inorder bounds
    if lo > hi: return None
    root_val = preorder[self.pre]; self.pre += 1
    root = TreeNode(root_val)
    mid = idx[root_val]
    root.left  = build(lo, mid - 1)   # left BEFORE right (preorder!)
    root.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
    return root
rules: Preorder[0] (then the next unused preorder element) is **always the current subtree's root**.
Locate the root in **inorder** to split into left subtree (before) and right subtree (after).
Recurse **left before right** — preorder consumes the entire left subtree before the right.
Build a **value → inorder index** hash map up front so each split is O(1) instead of an O(n) scan.
Assumes **unique values** (so the map lookup is unambiguous) and that both traversals describe the same tree.
whenToUse: Rebuilding a tree from two traversal orders (pre+in, post+in)
Any divide-and-conquer where one array names the root and another splits the children
Problems where 'first/last element is the root' plus 'find it to partition' applies
antiSignals: Only one traversal given (e.g. just preorder) → ambiguous unless it's a BST or has null markers
Values are NOT unique → you can't uniquely locate the root in inorder; need positions/markers
Preorder + postorder alone → tree isn't unique unless it's full (every node has 0 or 2 children)
You need O(1) extra space → recursion + map is O(n); a different encoding is required
remember.takeaway: Two traversals pin down a unique tree because preorder hands you the root and inorder tells you how the remaining nodes split into left and right. The hash-map-of-indices plus a single advancing preorder pointer turns the naive O(n²) recursion into a clean O(n) divide and conquer.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand what each traversal encodes (preorder = root-first, inorder = left/root/right) and can combine them recursively — plus whether you optimize the repeated root lookup with a hash map.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-scanning inorder for the root every call (O(n²)), mis-slicing the preorder ranges, or recursing right before left so the preorder pointer desynchronizes.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Use a value→index map for O(1) splits, drive recursion with a single preorder index instead of slicing arrays (avoids O(n) copies), and explain why left must be built before right.

problemStatement:
Given two integer arrays `preorder` and `inorder` where `preorder` is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and `inorder` is the inorder traversal of the ***same tree***, construct and return the binary tree.

All values in the tree are unique.
constraints: preorder and inorder consist of unique values
inorder is a permutation of preorder; both describe the same valid binary tree
understanding: We reverse-engineer a tree from two of its traversals. Preorder visits root then left then right, so its first value is the overall root. Inorder visits left then root then right, so once we know the root we can split inorder into the nodes left of the root (left subtree) and right of the root (right subtree). Repeating this on each half rebuilds the whole tree.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are all values unique?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's essential. We locate the root by value in inorder, which is only unambiguous when values are unique.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do both arrays describe the same tree and have equal length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. inorder is a permutation of preorder, so every preorder root has a defined position in inorder.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the input be invalid (not a real tree)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: We can assume valid, consistent traversals. We won't add validation unless asked.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I slice the arrays or pass index ranges?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Pass index ranges and a shared preorder pointer. Slicing copies sub-arrays each call and adds O(n) overhead per level.

examples.explanation: Root 3 splits inorder into [9] (left) and [15,20,7] (right). Recursing: 9 is a leaf; 20 is the next root with [15] left and [7] right.
Root 1 has nothing to its right in inorder, so its entire subtree is on the left, forming a left-leaning chain.

approaches.name: Recursion with Linear Inorder Scan
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to establish the core idea cleanly, then note the repeated scan makes it O(n²) and motivate the hash map.
hints: What does the very first element of a preorder traversal tell you about the tree?
Once you know the root, where is it in the inorder array, and what do the elements to its left and right represent?
Recurse: the left part of inorder is the left subtree, the right part is the right subtree. Finding the root in inorder each time is a linear scan.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the n recursive calls scans inorder to find the root in O(n) worst case → O(n²) time. Recursion depth and the slices add O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
This is the algorithm in its most transparent form, before optimization. It directly encodes what the two traversals mean.

**Step 1 — preorder gives the root.** Preorder is root, then left subtree, then right subtree. So the first element of the current preorder range is this subtree's root. Create that node.

**Step 2 — inorder splits the children.** Inorder is left subtree, then root, then right subtree. Scan inorder to find the root's position `mid`. Everything before `mid` is the left subtree's inorder; everything after is the right subtree's inorder. The *number* of elements before `mid` also tells us how many leading preorder elements belong to the left subtree.

**Step 3 — recurse.** Build the left child from the left slices and the right child from the right slices. Base case: an empty range yields null.

**Why it's O(n²).** Correct, but the `find the root in inorder` scan is O(n) and runs once per node. A degenerate (chain) tree forces n scans of length up to n → O(n²). The fix is to precompute every value's inorder index once.
approaches.insight: The two traversals are complementary: preorder *names* the root, inorder *partitions* the rest. Internalizing 'who is the root' vs 'how do the others split' is what makes every variant (postorder+inorder, etc.) fall out naturally.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
def buildTree(self, preorder: list[int], inorder: list[int]) -> 'TreeNode':
    def build(pre_lo: int, pre_hi: int, in_lo: int, in_hi: int) -> 'TreeNode':
        if pre_lo > pre_hi:
            return None
        root_val = preorder[pre_lo]
        root = TreeNode(root_val)
        mid = in_lo
        while inorder[mid] != root_val:  # linear scan → O(n) per call
            mid += 1
        left_size = mid - in_lo
        root.left = build(pre_lo + 1, pre_lo + left_size, in_lo, mid - 1)
        root.right = build(pre_lo + left_size + 1, pre_hi, mid + 1, in_hi)
        return root

    return build(0, len(preorder) - 1, 0, len(inorder) - 1)

Locate the root in inorder — this O(n) scan is what makes the whole thing O(n²).
Count of left-subtree nodes; used to split the preorder range too.
Left subtree's preorder immediately follows the root and has leftSize elements.

approaches.name: Hash Map of Inorder Indices + Preorder Pointer (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. 'Precompute value→inorder index for O(1) splits, and carry one advancing preorder index.'
hints: The slow part is finding the root in inorder each time. Can you make that lookup O(1)?
Build a hash map from each value to its index in inorder once, up front. Now splitting is instant.

Instead of slicing preorder, keep a single index that advances every time you consume a root. Because preorder is root→left→right, recursing left before right consumes elements in exactly the right order.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The map is built in O(n). Each node is created once with O(1) lookup work → O(n) total time. The map, recursion stack (O(h)), and output tree are O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Two changes turn the O(n²) draft into a clean linear solution.

**Change 1 — O(1) root location.** Before recursing, build a hash map `idx` mapping every value to its position in inorder. Finding where the root sits in inorder is now a single lookup, not a scan. This alone removes the quadratic factor.

**Change 2 — a single advancing preorder pointer.** Rather than computing preorder sub-ranges, keep one shared index `preIndex` that starts at 0 and increments each time we take a root. Here's why that works: preorder lists a subtree as root, then its *entire* left subtree, then its *entire* right subtree. If we always build the left child before the right child, the pointer naturally walks the left subtree to completion before it reaches the first node of the right subtree. So consuming `preorder[preIndex++]` as the next root is always correct — the recursion order keeps the pointer synchronized.

**The recursion bounds.** We now recurse over *inorder* index ranges `[inLo, inHi]`. The current root's inorder position `mid = idx[rootVal]` splits the range: `[inLo, mid-1]` is the left subtree, `[mid+1, inHi]` is the right. An empty range (`inLo > inHi`) returns null.

**Why left strictly before right.** The shared pointer is order-sensitive. Build right first and you'd hand the right subtree the preorder elements that actually belong to the left subtree — the tree comes out scrambled. The left-then-right order is not a style choice; it's required for correctness.

**Why no array slicing.** Passing index ranges and a shared pointer avoids creating O(n) sub-arrays at every level (which would reintroduce O(n²) work and memory churn). We allocate exactly one node per value and nothing else.
approaches.insight: The map removes the search cost and the shared preorder pointer removes the bookkeeping cost. Together they express the structure of the traversals directly: 'next preorder element is the next root; its inorder index tells me how the rest divides'. This index-map + global-pointer template reappears in the postorder+inorder variant (just walk the pointer from the end and build right before left).

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
def buildTree(self, preorder: list[int], inorder: list[int]) -> 'TreeNode':
    in_index = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(inorder)}
    self.pre_index = 0

    def build(in_lo: int, in_hi: int) -> 'TreeNode':
        if in_lo > in_hi:
            return None
        root_val = preorder[self.pre_index]
        self.pre_index += 1
        root = TreeNode(root_val)
        mid = in_index[root_val]
        root.left = build(in_lo, mid - 1)    # left BEFORE right
        root.right = build(mid + 1, in_hi)
        return root

    return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

java.explanation: Precompute value→inorder index once → O(1) root location later.
Take the next preorder element as the root and advance the shared pointer.
O(1) lookup of the root's inorder position to split left/right.
Build left FIRST so the pointer consumes the whole left subtree before the right.

pitfalls: Recursing right before left — desyncs the shared preorder pointer and scrambles the tree.
Forgetting to reset preIndex between calls (Java instance field) — stale state on a second invocation.
Rebuilding the index map inside the recursion instead of once up front.

commonMistakes: Re-scanning inorder for the root on every call, making the solution O(n²).
Recursing into the right subtree before the left, desynchronizing the preorder pointer.
Slicing the arrays each call (O(n) copies) instead of passing index ranges.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Right-before-left with a shared pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A single advancing preorder index assumes the left subtree is consumed before the right. Building the right child first feeds it the left subtree's preorder elements, producing a wrong tree.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
root.right = build(mid + 1, in_hi)   # consumes left subtree's preorder!
root.left  = build(in_lo, mid - 1)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
root.left  = build(in_lo, mid - 1)   # left first
root.right = build(mid + 1, in_hi)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Searching inorder every call
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Finding the root with a linear scan is O(n) and runs per node, giving O(n²). A precomputed value→index map makes each lookup O(1) and the whole build O(n).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int mid = inLo;
while (inorder[mid] != rootVal) mid++;  // O(n) every call

patternNote: Divide and conquer on traversal arrays. One traversal names the root; the other (or the BST ordering) tells you how the rest splits into left and right. The value→index hash map plus a single advancing pointer is the canonical O(n) template, shared with the inorder+postorder and serialize/deserialize variants.
